papers.title: EEG-Jev: A Unified Single-Pass Decision Model for EEG
papers.abstract: EEG analysis spans choosing alternatives, judging statements, and rating ordered attributes, requiring calibratable probabilities with explicit meaning. We present EEG-Jev, a unified single-pass decision model for EEG. Given an EEG window, a question and an answer specification, one forward pass returns a typed readout: CHOICE gives a candidate distribution, NOUL a proposition probability, and SCORE an ordered-level distribution and expectation. One checkpoint is trained jointly and evaluated once on held-out splits of 35 public sources. Core raw outputs reach 54.08% balanced accuracy on Stieger2021 motor imagery, 70.45% on Sleep-EDF-SC sleep staging, 72.11% per window at threshold 0.5 on CHB-MIT seizure detection with 0.825 AUROC, and 1.700 MAE on 0-10 ds005292 pain ratings. Prior correction and temperature scaling lower negative log-likelihood from 0.766 to 0.606 on Sleep-EDF-SC and 0.166 to 0.019 on CHB-MIT, while direct readout cuts batch-1 latency from 122.43 to 63.11 ms (1.94-fold) against a matched-backbone generative comparator. Interactive demonstration and aggregate results: https://neuroimglab.github.io/EEG-Jev/.

papers.title: The cyborg fly: reflexes survive engineered actuators, coordination needs stand-ins
papers.abstract: Two wiring diagrams now cover the whole central nervous system of an adult fruit fly: one female, one male. Can such a diagram, run as a network of spiking neurons, drive a body? And if we swap the body's muscles for engineered actuators, what survives? We ran both connectomes, BANC and MaleCNS, as leaky integrate-and-fire networks of about 160,000 neurons each, and closed the loop through simulated sensors, actuators and bodies for walking and flight. The actuators are port-Hamiltonian, so energy is audited at every step, and swapping one for another changes only a configuration file. Null networks shuffled at five levels, from the whole nervous system to synapse counts, test whether a result depends on the wiring. The wiring produced specific functions: sugar on the labellum drove the proboscis motor neuron, leg joints resisted imposed movement, leg circuits oscillated, a looming disc drove a take-off signal on its side (in MaleCNS), and descending neurons throttled and steered flight. The resistance reflex survived 20 of 20 actuator settings in MaleCNS and 19 of 20 in BANC, including a Hill-type muscle pair and a geared DC motor; the actuator set walking speed and energy cost instead. Coordinated six-leg walking, flight stability and the correction of perturbations did not emerge. Each needed a labelled engineered stand-in, which the connectome could command. Such stand-ins can also manufacture an apparent dependence on wiring: in a rebuild of a published closed loop, odour navigation came from a hand-written rule, and the network entered only through one valence number. The two animals differed on some functions, and the differences traced to wiring, such as a haltere drive of the flight power muscles found only in MaleCNS. A whole-CNS connectome, embodied, gives reflexes, rhythms and command signals, but not the coordination that turns them into behaviour.

papers.title: Morphogenic necking of surfaces
papers.abstract: Surface morphogenesis occurs across biological scales, from subcellular vesicles and cells to visceral organs, tissue organoids, and whole organisms. Since morphogenesis often involves changes in topology, a natural question is that of appropriate mathematical descriptions that provide an approach to topological transitions of thin surfaces. Here, we suggest a general intrinsic framework coupling morphogen organization to surface geometry. We propose a minimal geometric model in which smoothing competes with morphogen-induced deformation to regulate shape, while loss of this balance can bring a surface toward a topological transition via neck constriction. A simple dynamical model coupling a scalar field to the surface metric reveals two mechanisms: gradient-driven constriction at steep morphogen transitions and curvature-driven constriction near localized morphogen peaks. For frozen morphogen profiles in simple axisymmetric examples, the gradient-driven route gives exact algebraic contraction, while the curvature-driven route gives local exponential contraction.

papers.title: What time is it in Assembly Space? Cronin and Walker's "The Physics of Causation" fails elementary dimensional analysis (Comment on arXiv:2601.00515)
papers.abstract: Cronin and Walker claim that causation is quantified by an ``assembly index'', a count of the steps needed to build an object. Remarkably, they equate ``continuous time (as measured by clocks)'' to a multiple of the index, which is a dimensionless number. Their argument treats one parameter as simultaneously a rate, a time interval, and a pure number, and provides no timescale to convert index to clock time. This dimensional incoherence betrays, at best, an ill-conceived and ill-formed theory, and fatally undermines two central claims. First, the exponential weighting at the heart of what they call the assembly equation can be obtained only by supplying a timescale, which they never do, or by recasting clock time as a dimensionless count of assembly steps. In the latter case, their ``derivation'' trivially reduces to Bernoulli's seventeenth-century compound-interest limit. Second, lacking rates or energy scales, their account cannot predict how quickly, or under what conditions, anything forms, and yet formation ``in finite time'' is their criterion for distinguishing spontaneous from ``selected'' objects. Assembly theory is thus incapable of addressing causation.

papers.title: Impact of Taylor-Aris dispersion on chemical patterns in confined channel flows
papers.abstract: Chemical patterns form through non-linear interactions between different species. We study how confined channel flows affect pattern formation using the Brusselator as a paradigmatic activator-inhibitor model. An invariant-manifold method for slender channels reduces the advection-diffusion-reaction equation to one spatial dimension, with species transported at the mean flow velocity and molecular diffusivities replaced by the classical Taylor-Aris dispersion coefficients. We obtain the phase diagram as a function of the P\'eclet number (i.e., the relative strength of advection to diffusion), the channel slenderness, and the diffusivity ratio of the species. Our analytical results demonstrate that the classical Turing criterion can become inverted at large P\'eclet numbers and, thus, channel flow can trigger pattern formation even when the molecular diffusivities violate the classical Turing condition, and conversely destroy pre-existing patterns. Both predictions are confirmed by direct numerical simulations, which show advected stripe patterns, whose wavelength can be predicted by our reduced theory, as well as oscillatory dynamics. These findings highlight that hydrodynamic flows can modify chemical mixing and thereby profoundly affect pattern formation in channel geometries.

papers.title: Lattice models of chiral random motion: A short review
papers.abstract: Chirality, a systematic rotational bias, is ubiquitous in many random motion patterns, from bacteria cells, that swim in circles near surfaces and spinning colloids, to charged particles diffusing under the influence of magnetic fields. In two dimensions, chirality renders random transport \textit{odd}: the diffusion tensor acquires an antisymmetric part that leaves the mean-squared displacement invariant but modifies fluxes and boundary currents. Lattice models for random motion are a natural setting to study chirality, since they are exactly solvable, connect directly to heterogeneous media, cellular automata, and programmable robots, and in discrete time admit fully chiral limits with a localised bulk and edge transport. Lattice walks with a rotational bias have been introduced in different communities several times since 1960, yet without a common language or conceptual connection between them. Here we review these models from the perspective that on the lattice, chirality requires memory. Taking the recently introduced chiral random walk model as a template, we describe the walker with an internal degree of freedom. With a chiral biased updating rule, the full diffusion tensor of this chiral walker turns odd. Within this picture, we can unite persistent and chiral walks, run-and-tumble motion, and cyclic random motions in one framework. We discuss how the memory is followed into the environment; in Lorentz lattice gases, kinetic and rotor walks, and random odd environments; and into the path; in spiral self-avoiding walks.

papers.title: Snap-Through Symmetry Breaking in Multicellular Aggregates
papers.abstract: Symmetry breaking is a fundamental process in biological organization. Yet the physical mechanisms that control its onset in multicellular systems remain poorly understood. Motivated by gastruloids -- multicellular aggregates in which cells differentiate and spontaneously break symmetry -- we study a two-phase viscoelastic solid drop as a minimal model of tissue polarization. We show that elastocapillary competition fundamentally alters the classical engulfing transition of fluid drops. While symmetry breaking occurs continuously in the purely viscous limit, bulk elasticity instead leads to a discontinuous snap-like transition. We demonstrate that this behavior can be understood as a wetting transition governed by a spreading coefficient which depends on the drop size and phase volume fraction. Applying our model to gastruloids, we find a critical volume fraction for symmetry breaking, providing a self-organized mechanism for robust developmental timing. Our results identify a generic elastocapillary transition that enables spontaneous symmetry breaking in biphasic drops.

papers.title: Geometry and topology of DNA defects
papers.abstract: DNA defects arise frequently, either as a result of damage, protein binding or the action of molecular enzymes such as an RNA polymerase. Here we combine geometry, atomistic simulations and an analysis of real DNA structures to provide a quantitative characterisation of DNA defects and their dynamics. The composite order parameter describing defects geometrically is a backbone-to-base polar vector, together with a quaternion capturing 3D base orientation in a single strand. There are three types of defects: flips of the polar vector, stacking defects of bases, and composite defects encompassing both. All types of defects feature in realistic structures for DNA and have functional relevance. Additionally, biased molecular dynamics simulations of DNA with an imposed elastic deformation form flip or stacking defects whose abundance and dynamics strongly depend on sequence and type of deformation. Our results provide a link between geometry and biochemistry, and could also be applied, for instance, to identify defects in RNA molecules and nucleosome arrays.

papers.title: Optical-Memory Transport Imaging: A Transport-History Framework for Finite-Memory Tracers
papers.abstract: Finite-memory optical tracers encode upstream transport histories rather than instantaneous local flow velocities. We introduce optical-memory transport (OMT) imaging, a framework in which finite memory couples internal-state relaxation to transport through memory kernels. Under structured illumination, these histories are converted into a measurable complex spatial-frequency response, whose local transfer-function limit yields constant-velocity inversion. Fisher-information analysis establishes kernel-dependent information limits and design principles for finite-memory transport imaging. Using experimentally reported tracer parameters, we further identify representative velocity regimes and estimate the theoretical minimum effective photon numbers required to reach a given velocity precision. This framework recasts finite optical memory as a general, quantifiable resource for transport measurement rather than a source of bias to be corrected.

papers.title: Cell and nuclear shapes predict confined motility
papers.abstract: Cancer metastasis relies on an enhanced property of cells to migrate efficiently even through constrictions smaller than their nucleus. Both cell and nuclear morphology may influence this process. How these morphologies relate to the likelihood that a cell will transit through a constriction remains unclear. Here we combine microfluidic experiments with machine learning to predict whether MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells are able to transit through narrow constrictions. Cells migrate within vertically confined boxes, and may migrate into neighboring boxes by transiting through constrictions, requiring a deformation of the nucleus. Defining a set of 12 geometrical features derived from cell and nuclear contours, we find that their average values are not statistically indicative of whether or not a cell will transit. To overcome this limitation, we use trajectories to train classifiers and evaluate their ability to predict future transit events. We find that the cell area and cell circularity carry most of the predictive information and less circular cells are more likely to transit. Without retraining, the models also predict transit through narrower constrictions and in more adhesive substrates. Morphological features of cells about 30 minutes before a transit event proved most informative about future transit events occurring or not. Together, our results show that cell shape, readable from simple contour descriptors, contains a transferable but condition-dependent signature of imminent transit.

papers.title: Identifiability Limits of Physics-Informed Inference for Spatial Stochastic Dynamics from Static Snapshots
papers.abstract: Despite increasing scale and resolution, many biological measurements provide only a static snapshot of molecular positions rather than the dynamics that produced them. By combining flexible representations with mechanistic constraints, physics-informed machine learning offers a promising route to inferring these dynamics from static snapshots. Motivated by subcellular imaging of gene expression, we ask when a static spatial pattern of molecules can identify spatially varying diffusivity, creation, destruction, and boundary exchange, and how different inference schemes perform on the task. A structural identifiability analysis shows that distributed sources are non-identifiable, whereas a point source such as a transcription site can restore identifiability. These limits are further shaped by seemingly innocuous modeling choices: the boundary conditions, the spatial regularity of the underlying dynamics, and even the stochastic calculus convention. We then adapt several physics-informed schemes, differing in how they represent the solution and enforce the governing equations, and demonstrate effective inference from a single snapshot. Physics-informed approaches can thus recover spatial heterogeneities of biological dynamics from static data, but their use should be accompanied and guided by careful identifiability analysis for meaningful interpretation of the results.

papers.title: Frustrated neurons: Energy landscapes and relaxation dynamics in repulsive phase oscillators
papers.abstract: Geometrical frustration, a central paradigm in condensed matter physics, provides a unifying language for systems in which locally preferred interactions cannot be made globally compatible. Here, we use this language to formulate a minimal theory of frustrated neural timing, mapping repulsively coupled rhythmic units onto antiferromagnetic $XY$ models. In this formulation, the condensed-matter concepts of local constraints, degenerate ground-state manifolds, metastability, and quench dynamics are used to guide our analysis of structured neural phase dynamics. This paper analyzes a hierarchy of geometries, beginning with a triangle as the minimal frustrated motif with two chiral 120{\deg} timing states, then a tetrahedron whose reduced ground-state manifold consists of intersecting continuous branches associated with antipodal pairings, and finally a kagome lattice on which local constraints define a constrained three-coloring manifold. The kagome lattice reveals that zero-temperature relaxation suppresses global synchrony but typically selects low-energy metastable torque-balanced states rather than exact ground states. We then show how the phase theory can be carried back towards biophysical neural models by treating the minimal framework as an effective-interaction target, where geometrical timing frustration arises from preferred phase lags that become incompatible around closed motifs. Our results suggest that weak global coherence in neural systems doesn't necessarily signal disordered activity, but can instead reflect structured local timing order within a frustrated dynamical landscape.
